name: Rishi Sunak
role: UK Prime Minister (2022–2024); Chancellor of the Exchequer (2020–2022); Conservative Party leader (2022–2024)
summary: Sunak is a market-oriented, fiscally cautious Conservative who argues that free markets and a modest, enabling state are the best basis for growth, while backing a welfare safety net, a free NHS and pensioner protections. In office he tightened immigration and pursued the Rwanda removal policy, softened net-zero measures while keeping the 2050 target, backed NATO, Ukraine and Trident, and took socially conservative positions on sex and gender and on national culture while defending a multi-faith Britain.

universal-healthcare.rationale: Called it an article of faith for over 70 years that the NHS is free at the point of use and funded by general taxation, and raised a levy to defend that; the 2024 manifesto pledges above-inflation NHS funding every year.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Raised the National Living Wage to two thirds of median earnings (£11.44, extended to over-21s) and the manifesto commits to keeping it at that level, about £13 by 2029; he described it as ending low pay.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: In the Mais Lecture he said the free market is the best way to organise the economy and, more than any other system, delivers happiness and security for the greatest number.

public-ownership.rationale: The manifesto he led rejects Labour's plan to nationalise rail as ideological and says it would put unions in charge, and proposes Great British Railways within a reformed private-sector structure; limited to rail in the record.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Says he firmly believes in lower taxes and that the marginal pound is better spent by individuals; the manifesto rules out raising income tax, VAT, capital gains tax or corporation tax. As Chancellor he did raise corporation tax and freeze thresholds, which cuts the other way, so the answer is mild.

unions-good.rationale: Said the alternative to his plan gives more influence to vested interests and the trade unions, and the manifesto calls Labour's union rules a threat to jobs and competitiveness and vows never to introduce them.

property-fundamental.rationale: Listed protections for private property rights among the enduring principles of free-market economics that provide the foundation for growth; he did not speak of overriding it being hard.

regulate-corporations.rationale: The manifesto says Conservatives believe in reducing the burden of regulation and sets out a Brexit-freedoms programme to repeal or reform EU law; in speeches he contrasts agile UK regulation with top-down precautionary EU rules.

cut-welfare.rationale: Pursued welfare reform meant to save £12bn a year (tighter work capability tests, sanctions after 12 months, PIP review) and called benefits a safety net, not a lifestyle choice; but said he would not make the safety net less generous or balance the books on the vulnerable, so evidence is mixed.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Said protesters may criticise government but cannot call for violent jihad or for eradication of a state or any hatred or antisemitism, and the manifesto asks police to publish guidance on offences such as chants and symbols; he also defends free speech.

state-harmful.rationale: Described the role of government as setting the framework, stepping in when needed and stepping back when necessary, and led a government running public services and defence.

empower-police-military.rationale: Manifesto pledges 8,000 more police, new powers such as facial recognition, and defence spending at 2.5% of GDP by 2030, which he called the biggest strengthening of defence since the Cold War.

decide-locally.rationale: The foreword promises communities can decide their own priorities rather than having them imposed from above, and the manifesto offers devolution deals and local referendums on traffic schemes; he also centralised some choices such as a statutory school phone ban.

rehabilitation.rationale: The manifesto promises rehabilitative services (drug treatment, education, work) to cut reoffending but also whole-sentence terms and tougher sentencing so criminals repay their debt; evidence points both ways.

traditional-family.rationale: Described the family as the greatest institution of all, to be protected and strengthened, and the manifesto backs childcare and family hubs; he did not define traditional structures narrowly.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Cites equal marriage as an achievement of the Conservative governments and the manifesto says the party is proud of the Same Sex Marriage Act; he was not an MP in 2013 and abstained on the 2019 Northern Ireland act that extended it there.

gender-social-construct.rationale: Said biological sex is a reality, that the Equality Act should define sex as biological, and said it is common sense that a man is a man and a woman is a woman.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Spoke of a new patriotism, protecting heritage, history and the British way of life, and the manifesto promises to protect statues, monuments and memorials and to build a stronger national culture through National Service.

reduce-immigration.rationale: The manifesto states immigration is too high and promises a binding legal cap on work and family visas that falls every year, and records higher visa salary thresholds and the end of dependants for most students and all care workers.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Said the international frameworks on asylum are outdated and that he would revisit them or the ECHR relationship if the Strasbourg court blocked Rwanda flights.

free-trade.rationale: Called openness and free trade part of the enduring principles of free-market economics, and the manifesto points to the CPTPP accession and new free trade agreements with India, the Gulf and others.

nation-first.rationale: Said he would always choose national security over a foreign court's jurisdiction and applies a national-interest test to aid, but leads on NATO, G7, COP and Ukraine support; evidence points both ways.

open-borders.rationale: The manifesto commits to a binding cap, to remove illegal migrants to Rwanda and rules out any return of free movement.

limit-growth.rationale: In the Mais Lecture said the main challenge is accelerating growth and that growth restores faith in free markets; his economic priorities in office were growth and productivity.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Said Net Zero by 2050 stays but rejected going further and faster than other countries 'with ideological zeal', scrapping boiler bans, upgrade mandates and new green levies.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Called himself unashamedly optimistic about technology making life better, and said AI could solve problems once thought beyond us, though he also warned of its dangers.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Said his government is building new nuclear stations for the first time in thirty years, funded Sizewell C and promised two new fleets of small modular reactors in the manifesto.

revolution-justified.rationale: Said membership of British society depends on change coming only through the peaceful, democratic process, and condemned groups who reject that.

central-planning.rationale: Argued that the free market beats any other economic system and warned against government deciding which sectors matter or setting more prices, calling that a false route to growth.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Defends openness and free trade, but his government kept steel safeguards, planned a carbon border mechanism on imports by 2027 and offered to back carmakers if others break trade rules; mixed, leaning against tariffs as protection.

state-directs-investment.rationale: In the Mais Lecture he rejected the assumption that government should decide which sectors will be important, criticising corporate welfare and ill-thought-out subsidies.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Listed an independent central bank with a clear mandate for low and stable inflation among the foundations of a sound economy.

democracy-best.rationale: Said we should never cease to extol the virtue of democracy and the freedom it brings, and on losing office told the country that its judgement is the only one that matters.

right-to-secede.rationale: The manifesto says the Conservatives will oppose a further Scottish independence vote because the 2014 referendum was decisive, and commits to protecting the integrity of the UK.

political-violence-never.rationale: Said threats of violence and intimidation are alien and must be resisted and that change can only come through peaceful, democratic means; he backs Ukraine's armed self-defence.

military-superiority.rationale: Presented the 2.5%-of-GDP defence plan as the biggest strengthening since the Cold War to deter adversaries and keep the UK the largest European defence power.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Praised Britain's multi-ethnic, multi-faith character and said immigrants have written the latest chapter of the island story without giving up their identity.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Cited Adam Smith to argue that the desire to better the condition of ourselves and those we love is laudable, and called a system built on individual responsibility and free exchange morally right.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Described the industrial revolution as the era that made Britain a leading country, and expected a green industrial revolution to be a source of national pride.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Launched a plan to make science and technology the national purpose and an AI safety summit, favouring innovation over rushing regulation; he did not address disruption to institutions.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Closed the net zero speech with 'Pragmatism, not ideology' and said policy should follow a realistic, fair path rather than ideological zeal.

direct-action.rationale: Said change can only come through the peaceful democratic process, and his government passed the Public Order Act 2023 to curb disruptive protests such as Just Stop Oil.

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: Named the division of labour, together with free exchange and individual responsibility, as part of the morally right way to organise the economy.

harm-principle.rationale: Created a generational tobacco ban so that children now 15 or younger can never legally be sold tobacco, restricting adults' future choices partly to protect their own health, not only others from harm; smoking itself stays legal for current adults.

conscription.rationale: The manifesto makes National Service compulsory for every 18-year-old, but with a choice between civic volunteering and a competitive paid military placement, so it is not compulsory military service.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Said the Jewish people are under attack 'in their homeland', that the UK stands with Israel today, tomorrow and always, and described Israel as founded to ensure the Holocaust never happens again; he also backs a two-state solution.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Later position: rejected the idea that ever more spending regardless of borrowing drives growth, said it is wrong to burden future generations with debt, and the manifesto targets falling debt. As Chancellor in 2020 he ran large deficits for the Covid response and a stimulus (stamp duty cut, VAT cut, Eat Out to Help Out).

economic-freedom.rationale: Argued that political leaders must make market economies succeed in order to preserve the freedoms that only come from them, and that if growth fails faith in free markets and liberal democracy weakens.

national-self-determination.rationale: Spoke of Ukraine's sovereignty and independence as the cause it fights for, and backed Brexit as taking back control for the UK.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: The manifesto introduces local-connection and UK-connection tests for social housing; this is the only recorded step limiting a welfare benefit by connection to the country, so the answer is partial.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Said that people who can work should and are expected to, that someone supported by the taxpayer has an obligation to put in the hours, and set out closing benefit claims after 12 months of non-compliance.

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Said he would not ban new North Sea oil and gas, and the manifesto legislates annual licensing rounds and new gas power stations to back up renewables.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Said immigrants have integrated and contributed without being required to give up their identity, giving the examples of a practising Hindu or devout Muslim who is also British; the manifesto still expects integration into communities.

proportional-representation.rationale: The manifesto commits to First Past the Post for elections to maintain the direct link with the local voter.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Voted with the government to reject Lords amendments to the Overseas Operations (Service Personnel and Veterans) Bill, which limited prosecution of troops for past conduct abroad; a vote only.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Said that 'it is not the colour of your skin, the God you believe in or where you were born' that determines success, and the manifesto values a society inclusive regardless of sex, orientation, ethnicity or religion.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Argued on net zero that without the consent of the British people policy would face backlash and said the approach must have 'consent, not imposition', with Parliament voting on the plans.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: The manifesto rules out cutting Right to Buy discounts, protects discounts rising with inflation and promises to fight any local plan to abolish the right.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: The manifesto commits to continue implementing Minimum Service Levels legislation to limit the impact of industrial action on public services; it presents the law as already in force.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Called Britain the world's most successful multi-ethnic, multi-faith democracy, and the manifesto calls it a multi-ethnic, multi-racial, multi-faith success story.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Criticised the drift toward government taking a view on more and more prices in the economy as undermining the free market; he did not address food price caps specifically.

party-controls-media.rationale: Said his government is protecting a free press, repealing Section 40 of the Crime and Courts Act and ruling out Leveson 2 and any re-opening of the Royal Charter.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Backed Leave in 2016 ('I voted for Brexit, I believe in Brexit'), and the manifesto says he will not agree to anything in the EU trade deal review that infringes legal sovereignty or involves CJEU jurisdiction or dynamic alignment.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Called NATO the most successful alliance in history, committed to AUKUS and the Joint Expeditionary Force, and based troops in Estonia and Poland.

death-penalty.rationale: Asked about reinstating capital punishment, said 'that's not my view, that's not the Government's view'.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Updated relationships and sex education guidance with age limits, and wants parents to see all materials; he objected to gender activists hijacking sex education and to teaching gender identity, so he backs sex education only in limited form.

sovereign-debt-cancellation.rationale: The manifesto pledges to work through multilateral development banks to deliver debt relief; this stops short of cancelling poor countries' debts outright.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: The manifesto keeps the UK as one of the largest donors and promises a return to 0.7% of GNI only when fiscal circumstances allow, under a strict national-interest test, so the duty claim is only partly supported.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: The manifesto he led promises steadfast support for the Trident deterrent and its modernisation; he voted for renewing the UK's nuclear deterrent in July 2016.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Said an independent central bank with a clear, unambiguous mandate for low and stable inflation is essential, especially when inflation is high.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Criticised the EU's top-down, precautionary regulation and said post-Brexit the UK should be more agile so that rules encourage rather than stifle innovation.

collective-defense.rationale: At the Vilnius summit he recalled the 1948 pledge to come to one another's defence as the seed of the North Atlantic Treaty and said NATO is more important than ever.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Backed a peace based on territorial integrity and sovereignty, quoting the G7 statement, and said violent territorial aggression must not reap rewards; he did not use the word occupation for annexed territory.

no-bailouts.rationale: Criticised a growing tolerance for businesses reliant on taxpayers' support and never allowed to fail, calling corporate welfare unfair to taxpayers; he did not address bank bailouts specifically.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Introduced emergency legislation for Parliament to declare Rwanda safe and stop repeated court challenges, but also said the rule of law is fundamental and accepted the Supreme Court ruling; evidence points both ways.

patriotic-education.rationale: The manifesto promises to support teachers to uphold and promote fundamental British values and National Service to build national pride; it does not mention flags or anthems.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Described the aim of the Rwanda legislation in terms of a sovereign Parliament deciding a country is safe, and said he would not let a foreign court override Parliament's express wishes.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: The manifesto says the party has prioritised animal welfare and commits to banning hunting trophy imports and tackling puppy smuggling and livestock worrying.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: The manifesto says the party will always protect national heritage including statues, monuments and memorials and keep 'retain and explain' guidance under review to support preservation.

non-intervention.rationale: The manifesto commits to travel bans and sanctions on individuals and entities abroad and to work against global rollback of rights; he led arms and training support for Ukraine against Russia's invasion.

religious-nation.rationale: Held that Britain's national community includes many faiths (Hindu, Muslim, Jewish and Christian) rather than being defined by one religion.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: The manifesto commits to growing opportunities for NHS, charity and independent providers to offer services free to NHS patients, and to extending patient choice to more community services.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Said the free market correlates with higher living standards, longer lives and peace, and that history shows it best delivers security for the greatest number; he spoke of free markets rather than capitalism by name.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Treated the free-market system as the morally right and most successful way to organise the economy, with only limits to be managed, not a third course.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: The manifesto commits to protect people persecuted abroad for their sexuality and to run campaigns against such persecution, and says no one in Britain should be harmed or harassed for who they are.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: The manifesto commits to primary legislation so that sex in the Equality Act means biological sex and that a person can have only one sex in law, while saying provisions for those whose sense of self differs will remain and that harassment of anyone is wrong.

assisted-dying.rationale: Voted aye at the second reading (29 November 2024) and third reading (20 June 2025) of the Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill; the manifesto treated assisted dying as a matter of conscience.

islam-incompatible.rationale: Said the faith of Islam, peacefully practised by millions, is not the same as the political ideology of Islamism, and cited devout Muslims as patriotic citizens.

social-market-economy.rationale: Argued the market is the right basis but has limits, so government must support people through the welfare state, public services and education while guarding against a market society.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: Expanded the armed forces' funding and role, including a new military placement option in National Service.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Led UK efforts to expand NATO (Finland, Sweden) and set out a campaign for all allies to spend 2.5%, framing an axis of authoritarian states as the threat.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Quoted the expert statement that mitigating extinction risk from AI should be a global priority and hosted the first AI safety summit, while telling people not to lose sleep over it now.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: Wrote 'Biological sex is a reality' in the manifesto and committed to law making sex mean biological sex.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: Said his government would not allow the word 'woman' to be erased by health services and would protect female-only spaces defined by biological sex.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Scrapped proposed taxes on meat and flying and ruled out new green levies, a frequent flyer levy and pay-per-mile road pricing; he did introduce an Energy Profits Levy and plans a carbon border price on imports.

future-generations.rationale: The manifesto says the party is committed to leaving the environment in a better state for future generations and cites climate and nature targets, and he cited debt burdens on future generations.

arms-reduction.rationale: Raised UK defence spending to 2.5% of GDP by 2030 and promised £10bn for munitions, the opposite of cutting armaments, though he cites 'consistent with national safety' needs.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: Cited cutting the Universal Credit taper rate to make work pay as part of his Chancellor record; this tops up low-paid working households but he did not speak of tax credits as such.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: The manifesto pledges steadfast support for Trident and invests in its modernisation, and he voted to renew it in 2016.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: Objected that net-zero policies such as boiler bans, mandatory upgrades and car-sharing rules interfere too much in people's way of life and rejected them.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: The manifesto commits to mandatory life without parole for more of the worst murderers, whole-sentence terms for rapists and a 25-year term for domestic murders.

voter-id.rationale: The manifesto commits to maintain rules to tackle voting fraud, including the requirement to show ID, and to make veterans' ID cards valid for voting; it does not mention proof of citizenship.

international-criminal-courts.rationale: Said Russia must be held accountable for war crimes and noted Putin has been indicted as a war criminal, but called the ICC prosecutor's move to seek warrants against Israeli leaders unhelpful; evidence points both ways.

national-church-status.rationale: Described tolerance in Britain as underpinned by the established Christian church.

equal-conscription.rationale: The compulsory National Service pledge covers all 18-year-olds, men and women alike, though the military option is voluntary.

close-ties-china.rationale: Said the 'golden era' of UK-China relations is over and that China poses a systemic challenge, while keeping engagement where consistent with national interests; he keeps the US as the special relationship.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Pushed better targeting of disability benefits and reformed Child Benefit, but defended universal provision such as the NHS and the triple lock for all pensioners 'whatever it costs'; evidence points both ways.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: Said that telling children the system is rigged against them or that Britain is a racist country is a lie, and that success depends on hard work not skin colour; the manifesto also cites narrowing ethnic disparities.

notes: Evidence is from his own speeches as Chancellor and Prime Minister, the 2024 manifesto he led, and his Commons votes. Mixed points: as Chancellor he raised corporation tax and froze tax thresholds and ran large Covid deficits (furlough, Eat Out to Help Out, stamp duty cut), while later arguing against stimulus spending and for tax cuts; he cut the aid budget but the manifesto promises a return to 0.7%. Votes alone (assisted dying, Overseas Operations Bill) are medium or low. His Hansard speeches were not read in full (his major statements to the House on gov.uk were); theyworkforyou.com was unavailable (HTTP 503) and members.parliament.uk blocked scripted access, so the Commons votes API was used for divisions. Many topics he never addressed are left null.
